Probably not, at least not 100%.

**Why it's risky:** At 56 you're close to the stretch where a large drawdown does the most damage (sequence-of-returns risk). The S&P 500 fell about 49% in 2000-02 and about 57% in 2007-09, and it took roughly a decade in the 2000s to get back to even. If that happens at 60-65, you have little time to earn it back and may be forced to sell low to fund living expenses. The index is also concentrated: the top 10 holdings are a large share (roughly a third or more), mostly tech-heavy, and it's all US large-cap.

**The case for it:** Your money may need to last 30-40 years, so a high equity allocation isn't crazy. Over long periods, stocks have beaten bonds, and being too conservative has its own cost, since you can run out of money later.

**What would change my answer:** If a pension or Social Security will cover most of your expenses, you can work longer if markets crash, or you have a separate cash or bond reserve, a high equity share becomes defensible. If this is your main source of retirement income and a 50% drop would force you to change plans, it isn't.

**A more typical setup:** Roughly 60-80% equities at your age, spread across US and international, with the rest in bonds or cash covering a few years of withdrawals. An S&P 500 fund can be the US core of that. A 2035-2040 target-date fund is a reasonable benchmark, and most hold around 60-70% equities now.

If this would mean selling in a taxable account, the capital gains tax is a separate cost to factor in. In a 401(k) or IRA it isn't.

This is general information, not personalized advice. A fee-only fiduciary planner can model your actual income, expenses, and retirement date.
